core: Push factors as conditions at the place of origin that drive people to leave (e.g. lack of jobs, poverty, conflict/persecution, natural disaster, environmental degradation)
Pull factors as conditions at a destination that attract people (e.g. job opportunities, safety, family ties, better services)
The categories that factors fall into: economic, political, social/cultural, and environmental (with a demographic dimension sometimes added)
Intervening obstacles (distance, cost, borders, laws, physical geography) between origin and destination, attributed to Everett Lee's 1966 migration model
That a single condition can be a push in one place and a pull in another, and that migration usually results from an interaction of both forces plus personal factors
supporting: Lee's four factor sets: origin, destination, intervening obstacles, and personal factors; the role of perception
IOM's 'drivers of migration' as a complex interacting set of factors rather than a single trigger

claims.claim: Push factors are conditions at a person's place of origin that drive them to leave (such as food shortage, war, flood, poor economic conditions), while pull factors are conditions at a destination that attract them (such as more job opportunities, a nicer climate, or a better food supply).
Push and pull factors fall into recurring categories — economic, political, social/cultural (cultural), and environmental — so that causes can be compared across different places.

Everett S. Lee, in 'A Theory of Migration' (Demography, vol. 3, no. 1, 1966, pp. 47-57), organized migration into four sets of factors: factors associated with the area of origin, factors associated with the area of destination, intervening obstacles, and personal factors.

Intervening obstacles are barriers lying between origin and destination that a move must overcome — including distance, the cost of the journey, national borders and immigration/visa law, and physical geography; the concept comes from Lee's 1966 model.

The same broad condition can act as a push in one place and a pull in another simultaneously (for example, scarce jobs at the origin push while plentiful jobs at the destination pull), and migration typically results from an interaction of both forces rather than a single factor.

The International Organization for Migration frames the causes of migration as 'drivers of migration' — a complex set of interlinking personal, social, structural, environmental, and circumstantial factors operating along a spectrum between voluntary and involuntary movement — rather than as a single trigger.

Push-pull is an analytic framework rather than a deterministic law: individuals weigh identical conditions differently according to personal factors (age, education, family stage) and act on their perception of a place, which may differ from its reality.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many categories of factors to name
positions: National Geographic Education lists cultural, demographic, economic, environmental, and political categories
The NVCC OER groups factors on economic, cultural, and environmental lines
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the four widely taught categories — economic, political, social/cultural, and environmental — and notes that a demographic dimension is sometimes added, avoiding any claim that the list is fixed.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft contained only generic 'define the term and apply it' boilerplate with no substantive push-pull content; none of its specific claims were reusable.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Human Migration
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch. Defines push factors as forces that drive people away from a place (e.g. food shortage, war, flood) and pull factors as forces that draw people to a place (e.g. nicer climate, more job opportunities, better food supply); lists cultural, demographic, economic, environmental, and political categories. Page marked '© 1996-2026 National Geographic Society. All rights reserved,' so reference-only; supports the push/pull definitions and category set.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Cultural Geography, Ch. 3.2: Migration Drivers and Impacts
sourceRecords.provider: Northern Virginia Community College (Pressbooks) — Barbara Crain
sourceRecords.notes: Read in full via curl (browser user-agent) after WebFetch returned 403. Chapter '3.2 Migration Drivers and Impacts,' © 2024 Barbara Crain, licensed CC BY 4.0. States that push factors are events/conditions that compel a person to move from a location and pull factors are conditions that influence migrants to move to a particular location, occurring 'on economic, cultural, or environmental lines,' with economics the number-one reason. Supports the push/pull definitions and the category framework. Original prose used despite reuse rights.

sourceRecords.title: A Theory of Migration
sourceRecords.provider: Everett S. Lee, in Demography, vol. 3, no. 1 (1966), pp. 47-57
sourceRecords.notes: Citation verified via the Crossref API (DOI 10.2307/2060063): Everett S. Lee, 'A theory of migration,' Demography 3(1):47-57, 1966. The article's four-factor structure — factors at origin, factors at destination, intervening obstacles, and personal factors — and the concept of intervening obstacles were corroborated across multiple secondary summaries. Used reference-only to attribute the model and the intervening-obstacles concept; no text reproduced.

sourceRecords.provider: International Organization for Migration (IOM) — Migration Data Portal
sourceRecords.notes: Live page returned HTTP 403 to the fetcher; content read from an Internet Archive capture of the same URL. Quotes the IOM Glossary (2019) defining drivers of migration as a 'Complex set of interlinking factors that influence an individual, family or population group's decisions relating to migration, including displacement,' reflecting personal, social, structural, environmental, and circumstantial factors along a voluntary-involuntary spectrum. Used reference-only to support the framing of migration causes as an interacting set of drivers. IOM is an intergovernmental (UN-related) organization; sourceType recorded as government.
